name: Djoudj National Bird Sanctuary
blurb: Senegal River delta wetland where millions of birds stop after crossing the Sahara.

tip.title: Crash the fish
tip.text: Set Nile tilapia to -100% and watch pelicans, herons and crocodiles lose their main food, then the animals that eat them.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage: Djoudj National Bird Sanctuary

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong sun in a hot, dry region drives plant growth wherever floodwater keeps the ground wet.

nodes.name: Senegal River floodwater
nodes.desc: The sanctuary lies in the Senegal River delta, a chain of lakes, backwaters and channels that depend on river water.

nodes.name: Diama Dam
nodes.desc: Operating since 1988, the downstream dam changed the water balance and salinity, and invasive reeds and floating plants spread afterwards.

nodes.name: Floodplain silt and nutrients
nodes.desc: Silt and dissolved nutrients left by the river and by decaying plants feed the wetland vegetation.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead reeds, floating plants and animal remains, returning nutrients to the water and mud.

nodes.name: Southern cattail
nodes.desc: Tall emergent reed. Cattails (typhas) proliferated in the delta after the Diama Dam began operating.

nodes.name: Common reed
nodes.desc: Tall grass of wetland edges whose dense stands shelter nesting waterbirds; it has spread since the dam.

nodes.name: White Egyptian lotus
nodes.desc: Floating-leaved water lily of the sanctuary pools, recorded near the park.

nodes.name: Water lettuce
nodes.desc: Floating plant listed by UNESCO among the invasive aquatic plants that spread after the dam; warthogs are recorded eating it.

nodes.name: African savanna hare
nodes.desc: Grass-eating hare of the dry land around the wetlands.

nodes.name: African grass rat
nodes.desc: Common rodent of grassy, damp ground and an important prey item for many predators in the region.

nodes.name: Common warthog
nodes.desc: The best-recorded mammal near the sanctuary; it grazes and roots, and GloBI records it eating water lettuce.

nodes.name: White-faced whistling duck
nodes.desc: Abundant wetland duck recorded eating cattail; it feeds on plant matter in shallow water.

nodes.name: Nile tilapia
nodes.desc: Widespread African freshwater fish that eats plants and algae; a main food of fish-eating birds and crocodiles.

nodes.name: Egyptian mongoose
nodes.desc: Hunts rodents, birds, eggs and reptiles; GloBI holds records of it eating many of the local birds.

nodes.name: African golden wolf
nodes.desc: Opportunistic canid that hunts rodents and hares and also scavenges carcasses.

nodes.name: Nile monitor
nodes.desc: Large lizard of riversides that eats fish, eggs, frogs, small mammals and carrion.

nodes.name: Grey heron
nodes.desc: Wading bird that stalks fish, amphibians and small rodents in shallows.

nodes.name: Great white pelican
nodes.desc: Nests in the sanctuary; hunts fish, often in groups that herd fish together. Pelicans are among its most visible birds.

nodes.name: West African crocodile
nodes.desc: Large reptile reported in large numbers in the sanctuary; it is mainly a fish-eating ambush predator of the river and lakes.

nodes.name: Western marsh harrier
nodes.desc: Raptor that quarters reedbeds and wetlands, hunting waterbirds, small mammals and other prey; the best-recorded bird near the park.

nodes.name: African rock python
nodes.desc: Large constrictor; GloBI records it eating Nile monitors, and it also takes rodents.
